questions.stem: An IT operations lead asks Claude to turn a technical maintenance notice into a plain-language message for all staff. The original says the VPN will be down Saturday 22:00 to 02:00, on-call staff must use the backup dial-in during that window, and laptops not restarted by Friday will lose remote access on Monday. Claude's version reads smoothly: 'Some systems may be briefly unavailable this weekend. Please restart your laptop when convenient.' What should she do BEFORE sending it?

options.text: Send it as written, because the goal was a message non-technical staff can read easily and this one clearly achieves that.
Ask Claude to rate how faithful its simplified version is to the original notice, and send it if the score is high.
Check it against the original for every time, action and deadline, then ask Claude to put the missing ones back in plain words.
Send the original technical notice instead, since it is the complete and accurate version and staff can ask questions.

questions.explanation: Simplifying is where meaning drifts. The plain version lost the **window** (Saturday 22:00 to 02:00), the **on-call instruction** (use the backup dial-in) and the **deadline with its consequence** (restart by Friday or lose access Monday). Adapting for an audience changes vocabulary and structure, not the facts. The fix is to compare the new version with the source, list what went missing, and ask for a plain-language version that keeps every requirement.

whyWrong.A: Readable but wrong is not a successful adaptation. Staff would miss the Friday deadline and on-call staff would not know about the backup dial-in.
whyWrong.B: Claude's rating of its own rewrite is not evidence. A direct comparison with the original notice is quick and reliable.
whyWrong.D: The original is accurate but written for the wrong reader. Many staff would skim past jargon and miss the deadline anyway; the task is to adapt it, not give up on adapting it.

questions.mindset: Change the words for the reader, never the facts: check every date, action and condition survived the rewrite.

questions.stem: A marketing coordinator has two Claude drafts of a launch email to existing customers. Draft 1 is punchy and on length, but says the new feature is 'available on every plan'; the product brief says Pro and Enterprise only. Draft 2 gets plan availability right but is 40% over the word target and puts the call to action in the last paragraph. Which TWO actions are the BEST way to reach a sendable email? Choose TWO.

options.text: Choose Draft 1, since engagement matters most for a launch email and plan details can be explained later on the FAQ page.
Treat accuracy against the product brief as a pass/fail criterion, so any draft that misstates plan availability is fixed or rejected.
Ask Claude to merge the two drafts into one and send the merged version, as it should combine the strengths of both.
Regenerate both drafts several more times and send whichever version the team likes best on a quick first read.
Give Draft 2 targeted feedback: keep its facts, cut it to the word target, and move the call to action into the first paragraph.

questions.explanation: Comparing versions works best with **explicit criteria**, and factual accuracy against the source is a gate, not one preference among many. Draft 2 passes that gate, so the efficient path is **targeted feedback** on its real weaknesses (length, buried call to action) instead of starting over. Telling every customer a feature is on their plan when it is not creates support tickets and erodes trust.

whyWrong.A: A misstatement about who gets the feature is a factual error sent to every customer. Engagement does not outweigh accuracy, and a later FAQ will not undo the confusion.
whyWrong.C: An unguided merge can carry Draft 1's error into the result, and sending it without checking skips the comparison against the brief.
whyWrong.D: More versions judged on a quick read pick the most appealing one, which is how the inaccurate punchy draft wins. Volume is no substitute for criteria.

questions.mindset: Compare drafts against explicit criteria with accuracy as the gate, then fix the accurate one with targeted feedback.

questions.stem: A program manager reviews Claude's draft of a quarterly update for the steering committee. Paragraphs 1 to 3 are exactly right. Paragraph 4, on budget variance, is full of accounting terms the committee will not follow, and the closing paragraph just repeats the introduction. What is the MOST efficient next step?

options.text: Tell Claude to keep paragraphs 1 to 3 as they are, rewrite paragraph 4 for readers without a finance background, and drop the closing paragraph.
Regenerate the whole response a few times until a version appears in which every paragraph is acceptable to the committee.
Open a new conversation and write a longer, more detailed prompt from scratch so that the next full draft comes out right.
Reply 'This isn't quite right, please improve it' so that Claude can work out the weaknesses in the draft on its own.

questions.explanation: Targeted feedback ('keep X, rewrite Y for Z, remove W') protects the parts that already work and fixes exactly what is wrong, for a named reader. It is faster and more predictable than regenerating.

whyWrong.B: Each regeneration can change the good paragraphs too, so the manager may trade one problem for another and lose text that was already right.
whyWrong.C: Starting over throws away three good paragraphs and the context already built. A full rewrite is unnecessary when the problems are specific and known.
whyWrong.D: Vague feedback forces Claude to guess what 'better' means. It may polish the good paragraphs and leave the jargon in place.

questions.mindset: Say what to keep, what to change and for whom; don't regenerate blindly.

questions.stem: The head of internal communications says Claude's newsletter drafts keep sounding 'generic corporate', even though the Project instructions ask for a 'warm, upbeat and authentic' voice. Her team then spends 30 minutes per issue rewriting the tone. Which change is MOST likely to make drafts consistently match the house voice?

options.text: Make the tone instruction stronger and more specific with extra adjectives, such as 'very warm, genuinely upbeat, deeply authentic'.
Move the newsletter work to the most capable model available, since bigger models interpret tone adjectives more accurately.
Tell Claude to end each draft by checking whether it sounded warm and authentic and to fix any parts that did not.
Add two or three approved past newsletter pieces as voice examples, noting what makes them work, and keep a final human edit.

questions.explanation: Adjectives like 'warm' and 'authentic' mean different things to different writers. **Examples** are one of the most reliable ways to steer tone, format and structure, because they show Claude the target instead of describing it. A short note on what makes the examples work (sentence length, first names, light humor) helps it pick up the right features without copying content. A human edit stays in place because voice is a brand judgment.

whyWrong.A: Piling on adjectives keeps the same problem: Claude still has to guess what 'authentic' sounds like in this organization.
whyWrong.B: Model capability is not the bottleneck. Any model needs to be shown what this team's voice sounds like.
whyWrong.C: Self-checking against the same vague adjectives gives no new information about the house voice, so the result will look much the same.

questions.mindset: Show, don't describe: real examples of the target voice beat stacks of adjectives.

questions.stem: A training manager is adapting an onboarding guide for new hires in five countries, many of whom read English as a second language. Claude's draft is accurate for the US office but full of idioms ('hit the ground running', 'ballpark figure') and US-only references such as a 401(k) and the Thanksgiving holiday. The guide must go live in two weeks with minimal rework later. Which TWO actions are BEST? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask Claude for a plain international English version with short sentences, no idioms and terms defined, then check policies and dates are unchanged.
Keep the main text as it is so the tone stays lively, and add a glossary at the end that explains each idiom for international readers.
Have Claude translate the guide into each local language and publish the translations right away so everyone reads it natively.
Ask colleagues in the target countries to review a draft for clarity and for local details, such as benefits and holidays, that differ by country.
Ask Claude to make the whole guide more formal, because formal English is generally easier for second-language readers to follow.

questions.explanation: Adapting for this audience means two things. **Language**: plain, idiom-free international English with short sentences and defined terms, with a check that no policy or date changed in the rewrite. **Relevance**: US-specific content like 401(k) plans and US holidays may be wrong for other countries, and only people who know local practice can confirm what applies. Claude can draft the adaptation; local reviewers check the facts that differ by country.

whyWrong.B: A glossary puts the work on the reader, who has to keep flipping back to it, and does nothing about US-only benefits that may not apply to them.
whyWrong.C: Unreviewed machine translations of HR content, published straight away, may spread the US-only benefits and holidays into five languages without anyone checking.
whyWrong.E: Formal is not the same as clear. Formal writing often uses longer sentences and more abstract vocabulary, and it leaves the US-specific content untouched.

questions.mindset: Adapt both the language and the content for the reader, and get local experts to confirm what differs by region.

questions.stem: A supply-chain analyst asks Claude to condense her 12-page vendor risk analysis into one page for the CFO, who must decide on Thursday whether to renew the contract. Claude's summary follows the report's structure, walking through the methodology first and reaching the recommendation in the last paragraph. To save space, it drops the vendor's dependence on a single manufacturing site, which the full report rates as the most serious risk. What is the BEST refinement?

options.text: Ask Claude to shorten it further by cutting the methodology while keeping the original order, so the reasoning stays easy to trace.
Ask for the recommendation and decision first, then the top risks including the single-site dependency, with a pointer to the full report.
Send the full 12-page report with a short cover note instead, so that the CFO has every piece of information before deciding.
Ask Claude to turn the summary into a short slide deck, since executives usually take in visual formats faster than text.

questions.explanation: An executive reader needs the **decision and its impact first**, then the few facts that could change the decision. The single-site risk is exactly that kind of fact, so cutting it to save space removed the most important content. The refinement restructures the summary around the decision (bottom line up front), restores the top risk, and points to the full report for detail.

whyWrong.A: Keeping the report's order still buries the recommendation, and this option does nothing to bring back the most serious risk.
whyWrong.C: The full report is complete but wrong for a busy decision-maker. Giving someone everything is not the same as adapting it for them.
whyWrong.D: Changing the format does not fix the order or the missing risk. A deck with the same gaps is still the wrong summary.

questions.mindset: For executives: decision first, the facts that could change it next, detail by reference.

questions.stem: A customer success lead must tell customers that annual plan prices rise 18% from March 1, and that existing customers keep their current price until renewal. She asked Claude for a 'friendly and positive' email. The draft opens with 'exciting updates to our plans' and mentions the change only in paragraph three, as 'a small adjustment'. What is the BEST next step?

options.text: Keep the positive framing, because customers react better to upbeat news, and add the exact percentage and date to the email footer.
Ask Claude to make the email much shorter, so that more customers read far enough to reach the paragraph about the price.
Ask for a respectful, transparent tone, with the change, amount, date and renewal protection up front, then check every figure against the pricing decision.
Generate five more versions in different tones and let the team vote for the friendliest one before it goes out to all customers.

questions.explanation: Her original instruction ('friendly and positive') pushed Claude to spin bad news, so the draft ended up misleading in emphasis even if each sentence is technically true. Fitting the tone to the audience includes fitting it to the **situation**. For a price increase, customers need clear, respectful and transparent communication that leads with what changes, by how much, when, and how existing customers are protected. Calling 18% 'small' is a characterization the source does not support, so she also checks the figures and framing against the actual decision.

whyWrong.A: Hiding the key facts in a footer under 'exciting updates' reads as evasive, and customers who feel misled are more likely to complain or leave.
whyWrong.B: A shorter email that still frames the increase as small and exciting keeps the core problem: the tone does not suit the message.
whyWrong.D: Voting for the friendliest version optimizes for the wrong thing. The issue is transparency, not how cheerful it sounds.

questions.mindset: Fit the tone to the situation as well as the reader: bad news needs clarity and respect, not spin.

questions.stem: An HR business partner has three Claude-generated versions of an FAQ explaining a new hybrid-work policy to employees. She pastes all three into the chat and asks 'Which one is best?' Claude picks Version 2, describing it as 'the most comprehensive'. What is the MOST appropriate way to use Claude's comparison?

options.text: Accept Version 2, since Claude has just read all three versions closely and is well placed to judge which one is strongest.
Ignore the comparison entirely, because a model cannot usefully evaluate text that it generated earlier in the same chat.
Choose the shortest version regardless of the comparison, because employees read short FAQs and skip long ones.
Ask Claude to compare them against explicit criteria, such as accuracy to the policy and plain language, then check accuracy herself.

questions.explanation: 'Which is best?' gives Claude no criteria, so it falls back on something generic like comprehensiveness, which may be the opposite of what employees need. A comparison against **stated criteria** (matches the policy text, plain language, length, answers the questions employees actually ask) is a useful first pass. She still checks accuracy against the policy document herself and makes the final call, because a comparison is not verification.

whyWrong.A: 'Most comprehensive' was never her goal, and accepting Claude's choice without checking it against the policy skips the accuracy check.
whyWrong.B: This overcorrects. A criteria-based comparison is a helpful first pass, as long as a human makes the final call.
whyWrong.C: Length is only one criterion. The shortest version might leave out an eligibility rule or misstate one.

questions.mindset: Comparisons are only as good as their criteria, and the human makes the final call on accuracy.

questions.stem: From one open-enrollment fact sheet, a benefits manager has Claude produce three versions: an email to employees, talking points for people managers, and a summary for the external payroll provider. While reviewing them, she sees that the employee email says enrollment closes 'November 15', while the payroll summary says 'November 14 at 5 p.m.' What should she do?

options.text: Use the employee email's date in all three versions, since it is the version that the largest number of people will read.
Check the date in the fact sheet, correct the wrong versions, then cross-check the other shared facts across all three before sending.
Ask Claude which of the two dates is correct, and update all three versions to use whichever date Claude confirms.
Remove the exact date from the employee email and tell employees to contact HR if they need to know the deadline.

questions.explanation: When versions written for different audiences disagree on a fact, go back to the **source**. The fact sheet decides the deadline. Because one fact has already drifted, the other shared facts (eligibility, plan options, contacts, any other dates) may have drifted too, so she cross-checks those across all three versions before anything goes out.

whyWrong.A: How many people read a version says nothing about whether it is correct. If the 14th at 5 p.m. is right, every employee would get the wrong deadline.
whyWrong.C: Claude produced both dates, so asking it to pick one is not verification. The fact sheet is the authority.
whyWrong.D: Removing the deadline makes the email less useful and floods HR with questions, when the correct date can be checked in seconds.

questions.mindset: Many audiences, one set of facts: when versions disagree, the source decides, then check everything else they share.

questions.stem: A community nonprofit must share a grant outcomes report with local residents. The board-approved version uses phrases like 'programmatic outcomes' and 'beneficiary throughput'. The coordinator asked Claude to 'make it simpler', and got back the same wording in shorter paragraphs. Which refinement request is MOST likely to produce a version residents can actually use?

options.text: Describe the reader as residents with no sector background, and ask for everyday words, short sentences, clear headings and the key number explained.
Ask Claude to turn the report into a bulleted list, since bullet points are naturally easier for any general audience to read.
Regenerate with 'make it MUCH simpler' in capital letters so that Claude understands how important simplicity is to the task.
Publish the board-approved version unchanged, because any rewording risks changing what the board formally approved.

questions.explanation: 'Simpler' does not say who the reader is or what simple means for them, so Claude changed the layout and kept the jargon. Naming the **reader** and the **specific changes** (everyday words in place of terms like 'beneficiary throughput', short sentences, headings, the one number that matters) gives Claude a clear target. Adding context about who will read it and why helps Claude produce better-targeted output.

whyWrong.B: Bullets change the layout but not the vocabulary. 'Beneficiary throughput' in a bullet is still meaningless to most residents.
whyWrong.C: Capital letters add emphasis but no information. Claude still does not know who the reader is or which words are the problem.
whyWrong.D: Adapting the wording while keeping the approved facts is the job. If needed, the board chair can quickly confirm the plain version says the same thing.

questions.mindset: 'Simpler' is not an instruction: name the reader and what simple means for them.

questions.stem: A sales manager asks Claude to turn an engineering whitepaper into a one-page brochure for prospective clients. The draft is polished and persuasive, but says the product 'eliminates downtime' and 'guarantees compliance'. The whitepaper says it 'reduced unplanned downtime by 37% in a pilot with three customers' and 'supports compliance reporting'. Which TWO actions are BEST before the brochure is published? Choose TWO.

options.text: Keep the stronger wording, because marketing material is expected to persuade and prospective clients already discount bold claims.
Keep the wording but add a footer saying the brochure was drafted with AI assistance and that individual results may vary.
Rewrite each claim to stay within what the whitepaper supports, such as giving the pilot result with its context, in a client-friendly tone.
Strip all numbers and specific claims out of the brochure, so that nothing in it can be challenged as inaccurate by a client.
Have the product owner (and legal or compliance, if company policy requires it) confirm the external claims before publishing.

questions.explanation: Adapting technical content for a sales audience changes the **tone and emphasis**, not what the evidence supports. 'Eliminates' and 'guarantees' overstate a 37% pilot result and a reporting feature, and an external 'guarantee' could create legal exposure. The fix is to rewrite the claims so they are persuasive but supported (a specific pilot result with its context is often more convincing than an absolute), and to have the people accountable for the product and its external claims confirm them.

whyWrong.A: Overstated external claims can mislead buyers and create legal risk. Sounding persuasive does not justify saying something the evidence does not support.
whyWrong.B: A disclaimer does not fix an inaccurate claim. It labels the problem and still publishes it.
whyWrong.D: This overcorrects. A verified, specific result makes the brochure stronger, and removing it throws away the best evidence.

questions.mindset: Persuasive for the audience, but never beyond what the source supports.

questions.stem: An event coordinator asks Claude for a text-message reminder for workshop attendees. The draft is friendly and clear, but it is about 30 characters over her messaging tool's limit, and it says 'Room 4B' where the venue confirmation she has open says 'Room 4D'. The reminder must go out in ten minutes. What is the MOST efficient way to finish?

options.text: Ask Claude to write the reminder again from scratch, with stricter instructions about the character limit and the room details.
Edit the message herself: change the room to 4D to match the confirmation, trim a few words to fit the limit, then send.
Ask Claude to check its own message for any errors and shorten it, and then send whatever version it returns to her.
Switch to a more capable model so that future reminders come out within the limit and with the right room the first time.

questions.explanation: Refining output does not always mean prompting again. When the fixes are small, known and already checked against the source (the venue confirmation), editing directly is the fastest and most reliable way to finish. Claude's draft is raw material, not the final word.

whyWrong.A: A full regeneration is slow and may introduce new problems in a message that was nearly done. She would still have to check it again.
whyWrong.C: She already knows both problems and the correct room. Asking Claude to find them, then sending its version unchecked, adds a step and risk.
whyWrong.D: This does not help the message due in ten minutes, and a bigger model is out of proportion to a small, known fix.

questions.mindset: Match the effort to the fix: small, known corrections are faster to make yourself.

questions.stem: A project lead wants a casual weekly update to post in the team's chat channel. She keeps telling Claude 'don't be so formal' and 'don't use so many bullet points', but each revision just swaps one problem for another: fewer bullets but stiff headings, or a casual tone but a long report layout. Which refinement is MOST likely to get the result she wants?

options.text: Repeat the same two instructions again, worded more firmly, so Claude gives them more weight than its usual formatting habits.
Ask Claude to list everything it is doing wrong in the update before it attempts another revision of the text.
Describe the target: two or three short, conversational paragraphs with no headings, and paste an earlier update the team liked.
Accept the formal bulleted version, because Claude's default formatting tends to be the easiest layout for a team to scan.

questions.explanation: Telling Claude what **not** to do leaves the target undefined, so each revision fixes one thing and guesses at the rest. Clear prompts state the format and constraints you want, and examples convey a target more reliably than abstract description. A concrete description of the format and tone, plus a real update the team liked, closes the gap in one step.

whyWrong.A: Repeating the same instructions more firmly still leaves the target undefined: Claude keeps guessing what 'not formal' should look like.
whyWrong.B: A list of faults adds a step without saying what good looks like, and Claude's account of its own mistakes is no substitute for a clear target.
whyWrong.D: The team asked for something casual for a chat channel. Settling for the wrong format ignores what the audience needs.

questions.mindset: Say what you want, not what you don't, and show an example when you can.

questions.stem: An operations director is writing up a warehouse automation pilot. The same document goes to the leadership team, who need the ROI and a go/no-go decision, and to engineering leads, who need throughput data and failure modes. There is time for only one document. Which TWO approaches BEST serve both audiences? Choose TWO.

options.text: Write for an average reader, with a moderate level of detail throughout, so that neither group feels the document is aimed at the other.
Layer the document: a short executive summary with the decision and ROI first, then detailed sections or an appendix for engineers.
Keep only the engineering detail, because leaders can always ask an engineer to explain anything in the report they do not follow.
Use clear headings that say what each part is for, such as 'Decision needed' and 'Technical results', so each group finds its part fast.
Write the executive summary in the same technical language as the engineering sections, to keep terminology consistent throughout.

questions.explanation: When one document has to serve readers with different needs, **layer** it: the decision-level summary first for leaders, then the depth engineers need. Headings labeled by purpose let each group go straight to its section. Both groups get what they need from the same set of facts.

whyWrong.A: Aiming for an average reader usually serves nobody: too much detail for leaders deciding quickly, too little data for engineers.
whyWrong.C: This ignores the leadership audience. Making decision-makers ask for translations slows the go/no-go decision the document exists to support.
whyWrong.E: Consistent terms matter, but the summary is for non-specialists. Technical language there defeats the point of having a summary.

questions.mindset: One document, many readers: layer it and signpost it, so nobody gets diluted content.

questions.stem: A consultant asks Claude to turn an internal project retrospective into a client-facing case study for the firm's website. The draft reads well for prospective clients but still contains the internal project codename, the firm's profit margin on the engagement, and a candid note blaming a named colleague for a delay. What is the BEST next step?

options.text: Publish it as written, because the client already knows the project well and the candid details make the case study feel authentic.
Ask Claude to make the tone more formal, which should naturally filter out the informal internal details along the way.
Replace the codename with the public project name, but keep the margin and the candid note, since openness builds trust.
Remove the internal-only details, refocus on client outcomes, and confirm with the project lead (and client, if named) before publishing.

questions.explanation: Moving content from an internal to an external audience means deciding **what this reader should see**, not just changing the tone. Codenames, margins and blame aimed at one person belong in the internal retrospective. The case study should focus on the client's problem, the approach and the outcomes. Because it is public and may name the client, the project lead (and the client, if named) confirm it before it goes live.

whyWrong.A: A public website reaches far beyond the one client. Publishing the margin and blaming a named colleague causes commercial and personal harm.
whyWrong.B: A formal tone does not reliably remove content. The margin and the named colleague could stay, just written more formally.
whyWrong.C: Sharing the margin and blaming a colleague in public is not good transparency for this reader. It is information meant for internal use only.

questions.mindset: Adapting for a new audience includes deciding what they should and shouldn't see, not just how it sounds.
